html:
Meluhha was the name Mesopotamian texts gave to a land far to the east that traded with Sumer in the late third millennium BCE. Most scholars identify it with the Indus Valley civilisation.

Sargon of Akkad, around 2300 BCE, boasted that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at the quay of his capital. Magan is usually placed in Oman and Dilmun in Bahrain, so Meluhha lay beyond them, at the far end of a sea route along the coast.

The texts name Meluhha's goods:

  • Carnelian and other fine stones, and long etched beads.
  • Hardwoods and timber.
  • Ivory, gold and copper.
  • Exotic birds and animals.

Archaeology fits. Indus-style beads, weights and seals have been found in Mesopotamian cities such as Ur, and a cylinder seal names a "Meluhha interpreter". A village of Meluhhans may have lived in Mesopotamia. Ports like Lothal may have served the trade. Mentions fade after the Old Babylonian period, as the Indus cities declined.
sum: Meluhha was the name Mesopotamian texts gave to a land far to the east that traded with Sumer in the late third millennium BCE. Most scholars identify it with the Indus Valley civilisation.
